claim: Escherichia coli single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) binding protein (SSB) is the defining bacterial member of ssDNA binding proteins essential for DNA maintenance.
source: Escherichia coli single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) binding protein (SSB) is the defining bacterial member of ssDNA binding proteins essential for DNA maintenance.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about SSB's role in bacteria.

claim: SSB binds ssDNA with a variable footprint of ∼30–70 nucleotides, reflecting partial or full wrapping of ssDNA around a tetramer of SSB.
source: SSB binds ssDNA with a variable footprint of ∼30–70 nucleotides, reflecting partial or full wrapping of ssDNA around a tetramer of SSB.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about SSB binding modes.

claim: Single molecules of SSB-coated ssDNA exhibit intramolecular condensation that exceeds expectations based on simple wrapping transitions.
source: We directly imaged single molecules of SSB-coated ssDNA using total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy and observed intramolecular condensation of nucleoprotein complexes exceeding expectations based on simple wrapping transitions.
evidence: This claim is supported by direct experimental observations using TIRF microscopy and magnetic tweezers as described in the manuscript.

claim: In conditions favoring complete wrapping, SSB engages in long-range reversible intramolecular interactions resulting in condensation of the SSB-ssDNA complex.
source: In conditions favoring complete wrapping, SSB engages in long-range reversible intramolecular interactions resulting in condensation of the SSB-ssDNA complex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from force spectroscopy and TIRF microscopy showing reversible condensation.

claim: RecO and RecOR further condensed the SSB-ssDNA complex.
source: RecO and RecOR, which interact with SSB, further condensed the complex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers experiments with RecO and RecOR.

claim: RecOR functions in part to alter long-range, macroscopic interactions between or throughout nucleoprotein complexes by microscopically altering wrapping and bridging distant sites.
source: Our data support the idea that RecOR--and possibly other SSB-interacting proteins—function(s) in part to alter long-range, macroscopic interactions between or throughout nucleoprotein complexes by microscopically altering wrapping and bridging distant sites.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SSB binds rapidly and avidly to ssDNA generated during the normal processes of DNA replication, recombination, and repair.
source: Single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) binding protein (SSB) binds rapidly and avidly to ssDNA generated during the normal processes of DNA replication, recombination, and repair (Meyer and Laine, 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: SSB protects ssDNA from chemical damage and exonucleolytic degradation, removes secondary structure, and enhances the enzymatic activity of many proteins involved in DNA metabolism.
source: In doing so, SSB protects ssDNA from chemical damage and exonucleolytic degradation, removes secondary structure, and enhances the enzymatic activity of many proteins involved in DNA metabolism (Shereda et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The binding modes of SSB are sensitive to salt, temperature, pH, and binding density.
source: These binding modes are sensitive to salt, temperature, pH, and binding density (Lohman and Ferrari, 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: At low salt concentrations, where ssDNA is partially wrapped around SSB, cooperativity is very high or 'unlimited'.
source: At low salt concentrations, where ssDNA is partially wrapped around SSB, cooperativity is very high or 'unlimited'.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work on SSB cooperativity.

claim: At higher more physiological salt concentrations, SSB binds in the fully wrapped binding mode and exhibits 'limited' cooperativity, where SSB forms dimers of tetramers (i.e. octamers) along the ssDNA.
source: At higher more physiological salt concentrations, SSB binds in the fully wrapped binding mode and exhibits 'limited' cooperativity, where SSB forms dimers of tetramers (i.e. octamers) along the ssDNA (Bujalowski and Lohman, 1987; Lohman and Ferrari, 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Early electron microscopic visualization of SSB-coated ssDNA revealed a beads-on-string structure similar to those observed for nucleosomes bound to dsDNA.
source: Early electron microscopic visualization of SSB-coated ssDNA revealed a beads-on-string structure similar to those observed for nucleosomes bound to dsDNA (Chrysogelos and Griffith, 1982).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: At higher binding densities, SSB-coated ssDNA structures form smooth, contoured nucleoprotein complexes that are condensed relative to the contour length of the corresponding dsDNA.
source: These structures are observed at a low binding density of SSB; however, at higher binding densities, the structures form smooth, contoured nucleoprotein complexes that are condensed relative to the contour length of the corresponding dsDNA (Griffith et al., 1984; Hamon et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: High-resolution atomic force microscopy (AFM) imaging of spread SSB-coated ssDNA formed in low and high salt measured approximately a twofold difference between the contour lengths of the nucleoprotein complexes.
source: High-resolution atomic force microscopy (AFM) imaging of spread SSB-coated ssDNA formed in low and high salt, measured approximately a twofold difference between the contour lengths of the nucleoprotein complexes. This difference in contour length was proposed to reflect the partially wrapped SSB35 and fully wrapped SSB65 binding modes, corresponding to a site size of 35 and 65 nucleotides, respectively (Hamon et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: An additional, intermediate binding mode, SSB55, was observed in direct binding experiments.
source: It is worth noting that an additional, intermediate binding mode, SSB55, was also observed in direct binding experiments (Lohman and Overman, 1985; Bujalowski and Lohman, 1986).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: More than a dozen proteins interact directly with SSB via its short, unstructured C-terminal tail.
source: More than a dozen proteins interact directly with SSB via its short, unstructured C-terminal tail (Shereda et al., 2008; Wessel et al., 2013; Bhattacharyya et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In the absence of interaction partners or ssDNA, the unstructured peptide tail of SSB interacts with the subunits within the SSB tetramer.
source: In the absence of interaction partners or ssDNA, this unstructured peptide tail interacts with the subunits within the SSB tetramer (Kozlov et al., 2010a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: PriC remodels the SSB-ssDNA complex to create a DNA structure competent for DnaB loading during replication restart.
source: Direct evidence for such modulation remained elusive for many years (Shereda et al., 2008); however, recent work has shown that PriC remodels the SSB-ssDNA complex to create a DNA structure competent for DnaB loading during replication restart (Wessel et al., 2013) and that PriA modulates the SSB-ssDNA complex to expose a potential replication initiation site (Bhattacharyya et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: PriA modulates the SSB-ssDNA complex to expose a potential replication initiation site.
source: Direct evidence for such modulation remained elusive for many years (Shereda et al., 2008); however, recent work has shown that PriC remodels the SSB-ssDNA complex to create a DNA structure competent for DnaB loading during replication restart (Wessel et al., 2013) and that PriA modulates the SSB-ssDNA complex to expose a potential replication initiation site (Bhattacharyya et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: RecO catalyzes the annealing of complementary strands of ssDNA even in the presence of SSB, which otherwise kinetically blocks annealing.
source: RecO catalyzes the annealing of complementary strands of ssDNA even in the presence of SSB, which otherwise kinetically blocks annealing (Kantake et al., 2002); in this regard, perhaps RecO is mimicking the action of PriA (Bhattacharyya et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: RecO's annealing activity is essential for RecA-independent, homology-directed DNA repair that proceeds through the single-strand annealing (SSA) pathway.
source: This annealing activity is essential for RecA-independent, homology-directed DNA repair that proceeds through the single-strand annealing (SSA) pathway (Kantake et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: RecO stimulates RecA-dependent homologous recombination by acting with RecR and RecF to promote RecA filament assembly.
source: RecO also stimulates RecA-dependent homologous recombination by acting with RecR and RecF to promote RecA filament assembly (Umezu et al., 1993; Morimatsu and Kowalczykowski, 2003; Handa et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: RecR binds to RecO and enhances the affinity of RecO for ssDNA-bound SSB.
source: RecR, which does not bind to ssDNA, dsDNA, or SSB, binds to RecO and enhances the affinity of RecO for ssDNA-bound SSB (Umezu et al., 1993; Umezu and Kolodner, 1994); however, neither RecO nor RecOR are capable of physically displacing SSB from ssDNA (Umezu and Kolodner, 1994; Ryzhikov et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Neither RecO nor RecOR are capable of physically displacing SSB from ssDNA.
source: RecR, which does not bind to ssDNA, dsDNA, or SSB, binds to RecO and enhances the affinity of RecO for ssDNA-bound SSB (Umezu et al., 1993; Umezu and Kolodner, 1994); however, neither RecO nor RecOR are capable of physically displacing SSB from ssDNA (Umezu and Kolodner, 1994; Ryzhikov et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: When RecR is bound to RecO, it partially inhibits the annealing activity of RecO but stimulates both the rate of RecA nucleation and filament growth on SSB-coated ssDNA.
source: When RecR is bound to RecO, it partially inhibits the annealing activity of RecO but stimulates both the rate of RecA nucleation and filament growth on SSB-coated ssDNA (Kantake et al., 2002; Bell et al., 2012; Morimatsu et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: RecA does not interact with SSB, RecO, or RecR.
source: As RecA does not interact with SSB, RecO, or RecR (Umezu et al., 1993), this activity must proceed through a RecOR-induced conformational change in the SSB-ssDNA complex (Ryzhikov et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: RecOR stimulation of RecA activity must proceed through a RecOR-induced conformational change in the SSB-ssDNA complex.
source: As RecA does not interact with SSB, RecO, or RecR (Umezu et al., 1993), this activity must proceed through a RecOR-induced conformational change in the SSB-ssDNA complex (Ryzhikov et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and logical inference from the lack of direct interactions.

claim: The length of single molecules of SSBAF488-coated ssDNA shortened when the concentration of sodium acetate (NaOAc) was increased during buffer exchange at a constant flow rate and a constant concentration of fluorescent SSB.
source: When the concentration of sodium acetate (NaOAc) was increased during buffer exchange at a constant flow rate and a constant concentration of fluorescent SSB, the length of single molecules of SSBAF488-coated ssDNA shortened (Figure 1C, Video 1, and Figure 1D)
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: The fluorescent intensity of individual SSBAF488-coated ssDNA molecules remained constant when salt concentration was increased.
source: however, the fluorescent intensity of individual molecules remained constant (Figure 1E, Video 1, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that the protein had not dissociated, but rather redistributed, along the ssDNA molecule.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: When SSBAF488 was exchanged for unmodified wild type SSB, the fluorescence rapidly decreased as SSBAF488 was displaced from the ssDNA.
source: In contrast, when the SSBAF488 was exchanged for unmodified wild type SSB, which has a higher affinity for ssDNA, the fluorescence rapidly decreased as SSBAF488 was displaced from the ssDNA (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Wild-type SSB has a higher affinity for ssDNA than SSBAF488.
source: In contrast, when the SSBAF488 was exchanged for unmodified wild type SSB, which has a higher affinity for ssDNA, the fluorescence rapidly decreased as SSBAF488 was displaced from the ssDNA (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the displacement experiment.

claim: SSB tetramers can transfer between ssDNA molecules without proceeding through a free protein intermediate.
source: Stopped-flow kinetic studies have previously demonstrated that SSB tetramers can transfer between ssDNA molecules without proceeding through a free protein intermediate (Kozlov and Lohman, 2002a, b)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SSB tetramers diffuse rapidly on ssDNA and can 'hop or jump' across long distances of ssDNA via intersegmental transfer.
source: and single-molecule experiments have directly demonstrated that SSB tetramers diffuse rapidly on ssDNA and can 'hop or jump' across long distances of ssDNA via intersegmental transfer (Roy et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: When the salt concentration was raised to 100 mM NaOAc, the flow-extended SSB-coated ssDNA molecules compacted to ∼60% of the length in the absence of salt.
source: When the salt concentration was raised to 100 mM NaOAc, the flow-extended molecules compacted to ∼60% of the length in the absence of salt (Figure 2A, Video 2), and then returned to the previously extended length when the salt was removed from the flow chamber.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SSB-coated ssDNA molecules returned to the previously extended length when the salt was removed from the flow chamber.
source: When the salt concentration was raised to 100 mM NaOAc, the flow-extended molecules compacted to ∼60% of the length in the absence of salt (Figure 2A, Video 2), and then returned to the previously extended length when the salt was removed from the flow chamber.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: When salt concentration was raised to 400 mM NaOAc, SSB-coated ssDNA molecules shortened to ∼12% of the flow-extended length in the absence of salt.
source: Similarly, this condensation was also observed when 400 mM NaOAc was used (Figure 2B, Video 3); however, the extent of the condensation was greater, wherein the molecules shortened to ∼12% of the flow-extended length in the absence of salt.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Approximately 20% of the SSB dissociated in the 0→100 mM NaOAc transition in the absence of free protein.
source: In both experiments, the molecules were dimmer at the end of the experiment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), where approximately 20% of the SSB dissociated in the 0→100 transition, and ∼60% dissociated in the 0→400 transition.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Approximately 60% of the SSB dissociated in the 0→400 mM NaOAc transition in the absence of free protein.
source: In both experiments, the molecules were dimmer at the end of the experiment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), where approximately 20% of the SSB dissociated in the 0→100 transition, and ∼60% dissociated in the 0→400 transition.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The observed site size of SSBf increased from ∼43 to ∼70 nucleotides per SSB tetramer over the range of salt concentrations tested.
source: The observed site size increased from ∼43 to ∼70 nucleotides per SSB tetramer over the range of salt concentrations tested as expected
evidence: This is determined from the titration experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The amplitude of the fluorescence enhancement of SSBf increased dramatically with salt concentration.
source: however, we noted that the amplitude of the fluorescence enhancement increased dramatically with salt concentration, indicating the molecular environment of the fluorophore was altered (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Approximately 2 M NaOAc in the presence of 5 mM Mg(OAc)2 is required to dissociate half of the SSBf protein from the DNA.
source: The salt-titration midpoint for this experiment shows that ∼2 M NaOAc in the presence of 5 mM Mg(OAc)2 is required to dissociate half of the protein from the DNA.
evidence: This is determined from the salt back-titration experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The site size of SSB changes approximately ∼1.7-fold (43 nts to 70 nts) over the range of salt concentrations tested, whereas the length of the SSB-ssDNA molecules changes approximately ∼13-fold (from ∼6.5 μm to ∼0.5 μm).
source: This comparison shows that the site size changes approximately ∼1.7-fold (43 nts to 70 nts) over this range whereas the length of the SSB-ssDNA molecules changes approximately ∼13-fold (from ∼6.5 μm to ∼0.5 μm).
evidence: This is a comparison of data from Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: The reported change in site size for natural M13 ssDNA is only ∼2.2-fold (from 35 to 77) over a comparable range (1 mM to 300 mM NaCl), which is insufficient to account for the observed condensation.
source: We note that the apparent site size of SSB can vary depending on the ssDNA used owing to exclusion of SSB from regions capable of forming stable secondary structure (Lohman and Overman, 1985); however, the reported change in site size for natural M13 ssDNA is only ∼2.2-fold (from 35 to 77) over a comparable range (1 mM to 300 mM NaCl), which is insufficient to account for our observations.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature data.

claim: Mg(OAc)2 induces a large condensation of SSB-coated ssDNA nucleoprotein fibers that plateaus between 1 and 2 mM.
source: Mg(OAc)2 induces a large condensation of nucleoprotein fibers that plateaus between 1 and 2 mM, and results in complexes that are as short as those produced with the much higher monovalent salt concentrations (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Escherichia coli maintains its intracellular osmolality by adjusting the intracellular concentration of glutamate, which ranges from ∼30 to 260 mM when cells are grown in media containing from ∼100 to 1100 mM solute.
source: Escherichia coli maintains its intracellular osmolality by adjusting the intracellular concentration of glutamate, which ranges from ∼30 to 260 mM when cells are grown in media containing from ∼100 to 1100 mM solute (Richey et al., 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The intracellular free magnesium ion concentration is within the range of 1–2 mM.
source: Therefore, we also titrated sodium glutamate (NaGlu) in the presence and absence of 1 mM Mg(OAc)2, which is within the range of the measured intracellular free magnesium ion concentration (1–2 mM) (Alatossava et al., 1985).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: At low concentrations of NaGlu (i.e. below 100 mM), the condensation was dominated by the presence of 1 mM Mg(OAc)2.
source: At low concentrations of NaGlu (i.e. below 100 mM), the condensation was dominated by the presence of 1 mM Mg(OAc)2; however, the observed condensation became dominated by NaGlu at higher concentrations (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and 6).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The observed condensation of SSB-coated ssDNA became dominated by NaGlu at higher concentrations.
source: At low concentrations of NaGlu (i.e. below 100 mM), the condensation was dominated by the presence of 1 mM Mg(OAc)2; however, the observed condensation became dominated by NaGlu at higher concentrations (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and 6).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: In the absence of Mg(OAc)2, there was a log-linear decrease in length of SSB-coated ssDNA with increasing concentrations of NaGlu.
source: In the absence of Mg(OAc)2, there was a log-linear decrease in length with increasing concentrations of NaGlu, similar to our observation for NaOAc.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The shorter, more condensed SSB-coated ssDNA molecules likely represent the physiologically relevant condensation state as estimated by the in vivo concentration and composition of salts.
source: Extrapolating from this data, the shorter, more condensed molecules that we observe likely represent the physiologically relevant condensation state of the SSB-ssDNA complex as estimated by the in vivo concentration and composition of salts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and known intracellular salt concentrations.

claim: Force-extension curves of individual molecules of ssDNA show that the force required to stretch ssDNA increases with respect to increasing concentrations of NaOAc.
source: The force-extension curves of ssDNA alone show that the force required to stretch ssDNA also increases with respect to increasing concentrations of NaOAc (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Force-extension curves for ssDNA alone at salt concentrations greater than 25 mM NaOAc demonstrate hysteresis due to the formation of secondary structure in the ssDNA.
source: The force-extension curves for ssDNA alone at salt concentrations greater than 25 mM NaOAc demonstrate hysteresis (i.e. the force-extension curves obtained by increasing and decreasing force do not overlap) due to the formation of secondary structure in the ssDNA (Bosco et al., 2014) see also, (Zhang et al., 2001; Saleh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4C and supported by citations.

claim: Hysteresis was absent in the force-extension curves measured in the presence of SSB, except at 750 mM NaOAc.
source: Interestingly, this hysteresis was absent in the force-extension curves measured in the presence of SSB (Figure 4D), except at 750 mM NaOAc, the highest salt concentration that we used in our magnetic tweezer experiments.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The modest hysteresis at the highest concentration of NaOAc (750 mM) is consistent with partial dissociation of SSB at concentrations of NaOAc greater than 750 mM.
source: This modest hysteresis at the highest concentration of NaOAc is consistent with our interpretation that the decrease in the amplitude of the fluorescence enhancement measured during equilibrium titrations with SSBf is due to partial dissociation of SSB at concentrations of NaOAc greater than 750 mM (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from Figure 4D and Figure 3A,B.

claim: The absence of hysteresis in the presence of SSB is strong evidence that the structures are always at equilibrium, and that there are no kinetically trapped intermediates.
source: More importantly, the absence of hysteresis in the presence of SSB is strong evidence that the structures are always at equilibrium, and that there are no kinetically trapped intermediates, neither short range nor the more likely long range random interactions (Schaper et al., 1991), that would contribute to non-equilibrium behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from Figure 4D.

claim: The intramolecular condensation observed is intrinsic to a reversible equilibrium folding of the SSB-ssDNA complex.
source: We therefore infer that the intramolecular condensation that we observe is intrinsic to a reversible equilibrium folding of the SSB-ssDNA complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of hysteresis in the force-extension curves.

claim: The salt-induced condensation of the molecules measured in the TIRF experiments is most similar to the relative condensation observed in the magnetic tweezer experiments that were performed at forces between 0.1 and 0.5 pN.
source: Since the salt-induced condensation of the molecules measured in the TIRF experiments (Figure 4E, black squares) is most similar to the relative condensation observed in the magnetic tweezer experiments that were performed at forces between 0.1 and 0.5 pN (Figure 4E, orange and gray circles), we estimate that this is approximately the shear force applied by flow during TIRF microscopy within our microfluidic cells.
evidence: This is a comparison of data from TIRF and magnetic tweezer experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The shear force applied by flow during TIRF microscopy within the microfluidic cells is approximately 0.1 to 0.5 pN.
source: Since the salt-induced condensation of the molecules measured in the TIRF experiments (Figure 4E, black squares) is most similar to the relative condensation observed in the magnetic tweezer experiments that were performed at forces between 0.1 and 0.5 pN (Figure 4E, orange and gray circles), we estimate that this is approximately the shear force applied by flow during TIRF microscopy within our microfluidic cells.
evidence: This is an estimate based on comparison of TIRF and magnetic tweezer data.

claim: The salt-induced condensation observed with SSBf-ssDNA complex is in qualitative agreement with the data obtained with wild-type SSB.
source: Importantly, because the salt-induced condensation of the SSBf-ssDNA complex is in qualitative agreement with the data obtained with wild-type SSB, we conclude that the salt-induced condensation observed in Figure 3 and Figure 4D,E is dominated by intramolecular bridging in cis, mediated by oligomers of SSB, rather than any property of the modified SSBf (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a comparison of data from experiments with SSBf and wild-type SSB.

claim: The salt-induced condensation is dominated by intramolecular bridging in cis, mediated by oligomers of SSB, rather than any property of the modified SSBf.
source: Importantly, because the salt-induced condensation of the SSBf-ssDNA complex is in qualitative agreement with the data obtained with wild-type SSB, we conclude that the salt-induced condensation observed in Figure 3 and Figure 4D,E is dominated by intramolecular bridging in cis, mediated by oligomers of SSB, rather than any property of the modified SSBf (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of data from experiments with SSBf and wild-type SSB.

claim: The addition of SSB resulted in an additional 3100 (±550) kBT at salt concentrations from 25 to 250 mM NaOAc relative to relaxing ssDNA.
source: The addition of SSB resulted in an additional 3100 (±550) kBT (represented as ΔΔE) at salt concentrations from 25 to 250 mM NaOAc relative to relaxing ssDNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, open red circles, dashed line).
evidence: This is calculated from the force-extension data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Only at the highest salt concentration measured (750 mM NaOAc) was there a substantial reduction in the ΔΔE, consistent with SSB dissociation at these high salt concentrations.
source: Only at the highest salt concentration that we measured, 750 mM NaOAc, did we measure a substantial reduction in the ΔΔE, consistent with our interpretation that SSB dissociates at these high salt concentrations, but not measurably below 250 mM NaOAc.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The total energy contribution of SSB binding is nearly constant (i.e. isoenergetic) within error, with respect to increasing salt concentrations (up to ∼250 mM NaOAc).
source: While the total energy contribution of SSB binding is nearly constant (i.e. isoenergetic) within error, with respect to increasing salt concentrations (up to ∼250 mM NaOAc), the contribution of each individual SSB tetramer should (and does) vary due to the transition in the site size across the range of salt conditions.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The energy of SSB binding to ssDNA corresponds to ∼11 (±2) kBT per SSB tetramer (assuming ∼200–320 SSB tetramers per ssDNA molecule).
source: Accounting for the change in site size as the concentration of salt increases, the energy of SSB binding to ssDNA in our measurement corresponds to ∼11 (±2) kBT per SSB tetramer (assuming ∼200–320 SSB tetramers per ssDNA molecule), which is in reasonable agreement with the binding energy previously reported (Zhou et al., 2011; Suksombat et al., 2015).
evidence: This is calculated from the force-extension data and compared to previous literature.

claim: When RecO was added in a stoichiometric ratio to SSB, the nucleoprotein fiber shortened ∼10% relative to SSB-alone across the entire force spectrum, and hysteresis was not evident.
source: When RecO was added in a stoichiometric ratio to SSB, the nucleoprotein fiber shortened ∼10% relative to SSB-alone across the entire force spectrum, and hysteresis was not evident (purple lines, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The absence of hysteresis in the presence of RecO suggests that RecO functions primarily in trans to promote annealing of complimentary strands, but not in cis to permit formation of non-specific secondary structures.
source: The absence of hysteresis in the presence of RecO is interesting because RecO is known to facilitate annealing of complementary ssDNA in the presence of SSB (Kantake et al., 2002), suggesting that RecO functions primarily in trans to promote annealing of complimentary strands, but not in cis to permit formation of non-specific secondary structures.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from Figure 5B combined with previous knowledge.

claim: RecR forms oligomers (dimers/tetramers).
source: RecR forms oligomers (dimers/tetramers) (Kim et al., 2012) and interacts with RecO (Umezu and Kolodner, 1994), but does not interact with SSB, ssDNA or dsDNA (Radzimanowski et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: RecR interacts with RecO.
source: RecR forms oligomers (dimers/tetramers) (Kim et al., 2012) and interacts with RecO (Umezu and Kolodner, 1994), but does not interact with SSB, ssDNA or dsDNA (Radzimanowski et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: RecR does not interact with SSB, ssDNA or dsDNA.
source: RecR forms oligomers (dimers/tetramers) (Kim et al., 2012) and interacts with RecO (Umezu and Kolodner, 1994), but does not interact with SSB, ssDNA or dsDNA (Radzimanowski et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: RecR negatively regulates RecO-dependent annealing.
source: It also negatively regulates RecO-dependent annealing (Kantake et al., 2002) but promotes SSB-ssDNA remodeling in such a way that enhances both the nucleation and growth of RecA filaments on SSB-ssDNA (Bell et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: RecR promotes SSB-ssDNA remodeling in such a way that enhances both the nucleation and growth of RecA filaments on SSB-ssDNA.
source: It also negatively regulates RecO-dependent annealing (Kantake et al., 2002) but promotes SSB-ssDNA remodeling in such a way that enhances both the nucleation and growth of RecA filaments on SSB-ssDNA (Bell et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: When RecR was added in the presence of both SSB and RecO, severe hysteresis was observed in the force-extension curves.
source: When we added RecR in the presence of both SSB and RecO, we observed severe hysteresis in the force-extension curves (Figure 5B, compare solid and dashed green lines).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When the force was decreasing in the presence of RecOR, the force-extension curve was essentially indistinguishable from the experiment containing RecO and SSB.
source: When the force was decreasing (Figure 5B, green dashed line), the curve was essentially indistinguishable from the experiment containing RecO and SSB (Figure 5B, purple lines), but when the force was increasing, significantly more force was required to extend the molecule (Figure 5B, green solid line).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When the force was increasing in the presence of RecOR, significantly more force was required to extend the molecule.
source: When the force was decreasing (Figure 5B, green dashed line), the curve was essentially indistinguishable from the experiment containing RecO and SSB (Figure 5B, purple lines), but when the force was increasing, significantly more force was required to extend the molecule (Figure 5B, green solid line).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The hysteresis observed with RecR suggests that RecR bridges distant contacts, either through protein–protein interactions or by facilitating intramolecular annealing in cis of regions of micro-homology.
source: This hysteresis suggests that RecR bridges distant contacts, either through protein–protein interactions or by facilitating intramolecular annealing in cis of regions of micro-homology, and that these contacts are disrupted as the fiber is stretched by the magnetic tweezers.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from Figure 5B.

claim: The addition of salt induced hysteresis in the force-extension curve, wherein formation of intramolecular secondary structure accounted for approximately 1400 kBT.

source: The energy contribution of RecO to the SSB-ssDNA energy was modest, accounting for ∼250 kBT (or ∼1.2 kBT per SSB tetramer).

evidence: This is calculated from the force-extension data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When RecOR was bound to the SSB-coated ssDNA, hysteresis returned to the system, which is interpreted as a result of long-range, protein–protein interactions bridged by RecOR bound to SSB-ssDNA.

evidence: This is a comparison of calculated energies from the force-extension data.

claim: RecOR bridges distant SSB tetramers and those tetramers must be disrupted as the molecule is stretched by increasing force.
source: Interestingly, this energy contribution is essentially the same as the energetic contribution from SSB binding to ssDNA alone (∼9–13 kBT per tetramer, see previous section), indicating that RecOR bridges distant SSB tetramers and those tetramers must be disrupted as the molecule is stretched by increasing force.

claim: When incubated together, RecOR forms a complex that binds to SSB-bound to ssDNA, and in doing so, both modulates the wrapped-state, or binding-mode, of SSB in order to induce macroscopic changes and serves as a scaffold to bridge distant sites along the SSB-ssDNA nucleoprotein fiber.
source: We conclude that when incubated together, RecOR forms a complex that binds to SSB-bound to ssDNA, and in doing so, both modulates the wrapped-state, or binding-mode, of SSB in order to induce macroscopic changes and serves as a scaffold to bridge distant sites along the SSB-ssDNA nucleoprotein fiber.

claim: The macroscopic condensation of SSB-coated ssDNA could occur either through the association of stable octamers or through ssDNA by the direct binding of distant sites to a single tetramer.
source: This macroscopic condensation could occur either through the association of stable octamers or through ssDNA by the direct binding of distant sites to a single tetramer.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of condensation.

claim: The extent of condensation is greatest under conditions where ssDNA is fully wrapped around the protein in the SSB65 binding mode, making octamer formation more likely.
source: The extent of condensation, however, is greatest under conditions where ssDNA is fully wrapped around the protein in the SSB65 binding mode, making the former possibility more likely.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing greatest condensation at high salt.

claim: The addition of SSB (or SSB and RecO) eliminated the salt-induced hysteresis caused by formation of DNA secondary structure through intramolecular annealing in cis.
source: In our force-spectroscopy experiments, the addition of SSB (or SSB and RecO) eliminated the salt-induced hysteresis caused by formation of DNA secondary structure through intramolecular annealing in cis.
evidence: This is observed in the force-extension data from Figure 4D and Figure 5B.

claim: The change in energy due to SSB binding (when summed over a single molecule of ssDNA) is nearly isoenergetic across a large salt concentration range.
source: When we compare the energetic contribution of SSB binding to ssDNA, relative to the salt-induced effects on the ssDNA polymer energetics (excluding the contributions from long range secondary structure by comparing the 'relaxing' ssDNA force-extension curves), the change in energy due to SSB binding (when summed over a single molecule of ssDNA) is nearly isoenergetic across a large salt concentration range (Figure 5A, compare the slope for SSB, red-filled circles, to relaxing ssDNA alone, open black circles, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The isoenergetic landscape implies a homeostasis with regard to the energetics of SSB, relative to ssDNA, at physiological salt concentrations, making the absolute intracellular salt concentration nearly unimportant relative to other cellular processes working on or with the SSB-ssDNA complex.
source: This is both interesting and unexpected as it implies a homeostasis with regard to the energetics of SSB, relative to ssDNA, at physiological salt concentrations, making the absolute intracellular salt concentration nearly unimportant relative to other cellular processes working on or with the SSB-ssDNA complex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the isoenergetic behavior observed in the data.

claim: The net change in the microscopic binding modes of SSB makes it possible for all (or most) ssDNA to be effectively coated by SSB, albeit with each SSB tetramer engaged in a different number of nucleotides and a different number of SSB tetramers engaged at each salt concentration.
source: We propose that this relatively constant energy contribution across the ssDNA is made possible by a net change in the microscopic binding modes of SSB in such a way that all (or most) ssDNA is effectively coated by SSB, albeit with each SSB tetramer engaged in a different number of nucleotides and a different number of SSB tetramers engaged at each salt concentration.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism to explain the isoenergetic behavior.

claim: The sum of the energy changes for each tetramer is balanced across a wide range of physiological conditions.
source: In this way, the sum of the energy changes (see Suksombat et al., 2015) for each tetramer is balanced across a wide range of physiological conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the isoenergetic behavior and cited work.

claim: The 'isoenergetic landscape' is independent of salt only when comparing the SSB-ssDNA curves with the relaxing conditions for ssDNA alone.
source: Importantly, this 'isoenergetic landscape' is independent of salt only when we compare the SSB-ssDNA curves with the relaxing conditions for ssDNA alone (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2), where secondary structure considerations are experimentally removed.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The absence of hysteresis in the SSB-ssDNA curves shows that there is no long range secondary structure in the SSB-ssDNA complexes.
source: From the perspective of displacing SSB from ssDNA by another protein, this is the biologically relevant comparison because the absence of hysteresis in the SSB-ssDNA curves shows that there is no long range secondary structure in the SSB-ssDNA complexes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the absence of hysteresis in the force-extension data.

claim: When calculating ΔΔE relative to the 'pulling' condition with ssDNA alone, the ΔΔE decreases until it becomes negative (and therefore unfavorable) at approximately 400 mM NaOAc.
source: When we calculate the ΔΔE relative to the 'pulling' condition with ssDNA alone where the contributions of secondary structure are clearly evident (Figure 5A, solid black circles and Figure 5—figure supplement 2, solid red circles, solid red line), the ΔΔE decreases until it becomes negative (and therefore unfavorable) at approximately 400 mM NaOAc, corresponding to a concentration of salt where secondary structure may become more stable than the SSB–ssDNA interaction (consistent with our observations in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is calculated from the data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Previous AFM imaging of SSB bound to M13mp7 ssDNA measured contour lengths of SSB-ssDNA of ∼920 nm in the low salt, 35-nucleotide binding mode, and 560 nm in the high salt, 65-nucleotide binding mode.
source: Previous AFM imaging of SSB bound to M13mp7 ssDNA (7249 nts) measured contour lengths of SSB-ssDNA of ∼920 nm in the low salt, 35-nucleotide binding mode, and 560 nm in the high salt, 65-nucleotide binding mode; this change represents a 1.6-fold increase upon going from high to low salt, or a decrease of 60% upon going from low to high salt (Hamon et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The previous AFM measurements represent a 1.6-fold increase in length upon going from high to low salt, or a decrease of 60% upon going from low to high salt.
source: Previous AFM imaging of SSB bound to M13mp7 ssDNA (7249 nts) measured contour lengths of SSB-ssDNA of ∼920 nm in the low salt, 35-nucleotide binding mode, and 560 nm in the high salt, 65-nucleotide binding mode; this change represents a 1.6-fold increase upon going from high to low salt, or a decrease of 60% upon going from low to high salt (Hamon et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the cited AFM data.

claim: The authors expected their SSB-ssDNA would be approximately 6.1 μm long in low salt and compacted by 1.6-fold to approximately 3.7 μm long in high salt (up to ∼300 mM Na+).
source: Since denatured λ-phage DNA is 6.6-fold longer than M13mp7 ssDNA, we expected our SSB-ssDNA would be approximately 6.1 μm long in low salt and compacted by 1.6-fold to approximately 3.7 μm long in high salt (up to ∼300 mM Na+); however, we observed an approximately fourfold compaction over this range.
evidence: This is an expectation based on previous AFM data and the length of their DNA substrate.

claim: The authors observed an approximately fourfold compaction over the range up to ∼300 mM Na+.
source: Since denatured λ-phage DNA is 6.6-fold longer than M13mp7 ssDNA, we expected our SSB-ssDNA would be approximately 6.1 μm long in low salt and compacted by 1.6-fold to approximately 3.7 μm long in high salt (up to ∼300 mM Na+); however, we observed an approximately fourfold compaction over this range.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: A substantially greater degree of compaction of the complexes was measured upon further increase in salt concentration – from 6.5 μm in the absence of salt to 0.5 μm at 750 mM NaOAc – which is a 13-fold compaction.
source: A substantially greater degree of compaction of the complexes was measured upon further increase in salt concentration – from 6.5 μm in the absence of salt to 0.5 μm at 750 mM NaOAc – which is a 13-fold compaction.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: If the site size was the dominant factor determining the condensation state of SSB-coated ssDNA, then the maximum change in length should be approximately twofold.
source: If the site size was the dominant factor determining the condensation state of SSB-coated ssDNA, then the maximum change in length should be approximately twofold, yet we measure a ∼13-fold decrease in length.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the known site size changes.

claim: SSB forms octamers at higher salt concentrations which might serve as an intramolecular bridges between distant sites along the ssDNA resulting in the condensation observed.
source: We propose that an explanation derives from the fact that SSB does not simply bind to ssDNA as an array of globular units, but instead exhibits limited cooperativity between tetramers, at higher salt concentrations, where it also forms octamers (Lohman and Bujalowski, 1988; Bujalowski and Lohman, 1989a, b) which might serve as an intramolecular bridges between distant sites along the ssDNA resulting in the condensation that we observe (Chrysogelos and Griffith, 1982; Griffith et al., 1984; Hamon et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The population of the various SSB-binding modes depends not only on intracellular solution conditions, but also on the SSB concentration itself due to the established effects of 'competition' between DNA-binding modes with different site sizes, affinities, and cooperativities.
source: Although the molecular nature of the condensing species is unknown, we also note that the population of the various SSB-binding modes depends not only on intracellular solution conditions, but also on the SSB concentration itself due to the established effects of 'competition' between DNA-binding modes with different site sizes, affinities, and cooperativities (Schwarz and Stankowski, 1979; Bujalowski et al., 1988); therefore, with SSB in excess over ssDNA – which is the cellular situation – multiple modes coexist and may serve to keep the amounts of bound SSB nearly constant.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: With SSB in excess over ssDNA – which is the cellular situation – multiple modes coexist and may serve to keep the amounts of bound SSB nearly constant.
source: Although the molecular nature of the condensing species is unknown, we also note that the population of the various SSB-binding modes depends not only on intracellular solution conditions, but also on the SSB concentration itself due to the established effects of 'competition' between DNA-binding modes with different site sizes, affinities, and cooperativities (Schwarz and Stankowski, 1979; Bujalowski et al., 1988); therefore, with SSB in excess over ssDNA – which is the cellular situation – multiple modes coexist and may serve to keep the amounts of bound SSB nearly constant.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited work and knowledge of cellular conditions.

claim: The high degree of salt-induced compaction of SSB-ssDNA observed is in good qualitative agreement with early ultracentrifugation experiments performed with SSB-saturated M13-phage ssDNA.
source: Finally, although the high degree of salt-induced compaction of SSB-ssDNA that we observed was surprising based on previous AFM and EM studies, our results are in good qualitative agreement with early, largely unexplained, ultracentrifugation experiments performed with SSB-saturated M13-phage ssDNA (Schaper et al., 1991): our changes in length with salt concentration map exactly on the reported changes in sedimentation coefficients for the SSB-M13 ssDNA complexes.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature data.

claim: The changes in length with salt concentration map exactly on the reported changes in sedimentation coefficients for the SSB-M13 ssDNA complexes from ultracentrifugation experiments.
source: Finally, although the high degree of salt-induced compaction of SSB-ssDNA that we observed was surprising based on previous AFM and EM studies, our results are in good qualitative agreement with early, largely unexplained, ultracentrifugation experiments performed with SSB-saturated M13-phage ssDNA (Schaper et al., 1991): our changes in length with salt concentration map exactly on the reported changes in sedimentation coefficients for the SSB-M13 ssDNA complexes.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature data.

claim: The force-extension measurements of unlabeled, wild-type SSB recapitulates the relative condensation of SSBf-coated ssDNA observed in the direct visualization experiments.
source: Importantly, the force-extension measurements of unlabeled, wild-type SSB recapitulates the relative condensation of SSBf-coated ssDNA observed in the direct visualization experiments, indicating that the observed condensation of the fluorescently modified nucleoprotein complex in Figure 1C and Figure 3C–G is not a consequence of using modified SSB, SSBAF488, or SSBf, but rather is due to an intrinsic, salt-induced conformational change resulting in intramolecular re-organization along the nucleoprotein fiber.
evidence: This is a comparison of data from experiments with wild-type SSB and modified SSB.

claim: The observed condensation of the fluorescently modified nucleoprotein complex is not a consequence of using modified SSB, but rather is due to an intrinsic, salt-induced conformational change resulting in intramolecular re-organization along the nucleoprotein fiber.
source: Importantly, the force-extension measurements of unlabeled, wild-type SSB recapitulates the relative condensation of SSBf-coated ssDNA observed in the direct visualization experiments, indicating that the observed condensation of the fluorescently modified nucleoprotein complex in Figure 1C and Figure 3C–G is not a consequence of using modified SSB, SSBAF488, or SSBf, but rather is due to an intrinsic, salt-induced conformational change resulting in intramolecular re-organization along the nucleoprotein fiber.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of data from experiments with wild-type SSB and modified SSB.

claim: The absence of hysteresis in force-extension curves in the presence of SSB is strong evidence that the intramolecular condensation observed is not due to the formation of distant ssDNA–ssDNA contacts, but rather is driven by the microscopic reorganization of SSB along the ssDNA.
source: The absence of hysteresis in our force-extension curves in the presence of SSB is strong evidence that the intramolecular condensation that we observe is not due to the formation of distant ssDNA–ssDNA contacts, but rather is driven by the microscopic reorganization of SSB along the ssDNA, which in turn contributes to a macroscopic folding of the molecule.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the absence of hysteresis in the force-extension data.

claim: The microscopic reorganization of SSB along the ssDNA contributes to a macroscopic folding of the molecule.

source: First, dimerization of SSB tetramers (i.e. octamer formation) is a well-established phenomenon at increasing but still physiologically relevant intracellular salt concentrations (Chrysogelos and Griffith, 1982; Bujalowski and Lohman, 1987), which can linearly vary from 0.23 to 0.93 molal K+ ion and from 0.03 to 0.26 molal glutamate ion in response to changes in the osmolality of the growth medium (Richey et al., 1987) see also, (Epstein and Schultz, 1965) (Epstein and Schultz, 1966).

source: Second, SSB exhibits long-range, intersegmental transfer (Lee et al., 2014), the latter of which likely proceeds through direct, tetramer transfer within a ternary intermediate comprising SSB and two ssDNA molecules without proceeding through a free-protein intermediate (Kozlov and Lohman, 2002a, b).

source: This property of SSB is possible owing to multiple, high affinity binding sites distributed around the tetramer, or as the case may be in the high-salt mode, octamers.

claim: The intramolecular condensation observed provides evidence that the sum of transient interactions across the SSB-ssDNA fiber might explain how many SSB tetramers can simultaneously engage in distant ssDNA sites to contribute to an intramolecular, folded polymer that is highly dynamic and 'fluid'.
source: This phenomenon has primarily been described as a transient intermediate during rapid, stopped flow kinetics; however, we believe that the intramolecular condensation that we observe here provides evidence that the sum of these transient interactions across the SSB-ssDNA fiber might explain how many SSB tetramers can simultaneously engage in distant ssDNA sites to contribute to an intramolecular, folded polymer that is highly dynamic and 'fluid', undergoing constant, steady–steady state protein turnover and diffusion at equilibrium.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The SSB-ssDNA polymer undergoes constant, steady–steady state protein turnover and diffusion at equilibrium.
source: This phenomenon has primarily been described as a transient intermediate during rapid, stopped flow kinetics; however, we believe that the intramolecular condensation that we observe here provides evidence that the sum of these transient interactions across the SSB-ssDNA fiber might explain how many SSB tetramers can simultaneously engage in distant ssDNA sites to contribute to an intramolecular, folded polymer that is highly dynamic and 'fluid', undergoing constant, steady–steady state protein turnover and diffusion at equilibrium.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The rapid exchange of SSB protein and the absence of net protein loss under steady-state conditions corroborate the dynamic nature of the SSB-ssDNA complex.
source: This is corroborated by the rapid exchange of SSB protein (Figure 1F) and the absence of net protein loss under steady-state conditions (Figure 1D–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), but the rapid dissociation in the absence of free protein during salt-jump experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), as well as the ability of SSB labeled with different fluorophores to exchange and form mixed complexes (JCB, unpublished observations), a phenomenon also demonstrated for eukaryotic RPA (Gibb et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the manuscript and cited work.

claim: SSB labeled with different fluorophores can exchange and form mixed complexes.
source: This is corroborated by the rapid exchange of SSB protein (Figure 1F) and the absence of net protein loss under steady-state conditions (Figure 1D–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), but the rapid dissociation in the absence of free protein during salt-jump experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), as well as the ability of SSB labeled with different fluorophores to exchange and form mixed complexes (JCB, unpublished observations), a phenomenon also demonstrated for eukaryotic RPA (Gibb et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as unpublished observations and compared to cited work on RPA.

claim: Eukaryotic RPA can exchange and form mixed complexes.
source: This is corroborated by the rapid exchange of SSB protein (Figure 1F) and the absence of net protein loss under steady-state conditions (Figure 1D–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), but the rapid dissociation in the absence of free protein during salt-jump experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), as well as the ability of SSB labeled with different fluorophores to exchange and form mixed complexes (JCB, unpublished observations), a phenomenon also demonstrated for eukaryotic RPA (Gibb et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Similar to nucleosomes, SSB binds and wraps a DNA polymer around itself (albeit ssDNA instead of dsDNA), interacts with dozens of proteins via a short acidic peptide tail, and exhibits complex cooperative and anti-cooperative behavior that is modulated by salt concentration.
source: Similar to nucleosomes, SSB binds and wraps a DNA polymer around itself (albeit ssDNA instead of dsDNA), interacts with dozens of proteins via a short acidic peptide tail, and exhibits complex cooperative and anti-cooperative behavior that is modulated by salt concentration.
evidence: This is a comparison drawing on established knowledge about SSB and nucleosomes.

claim: The observation that SSB-ssDNA is macroscopically organized and regulated through microscopic interactions is surprisingly similar to the most basic organization of eukaryotic chromatin.
source: Our observation that SSB-ssDNA is macroscopically organized and regulated through microscopic interactions is surprisingly similar to the most basic organization of eukaryotic chromatin and highlights the important role of SSB, not simply as a kinetic trap for ssDNA, but as an organizational and regulatory scaffold during DNA metabolism (Shereda et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data and comparison to chromatin organization.

claim: SSB plays an important role not simply as a kinetic trap for ssDNA, but as an organizational and regulatory scaffold during DNA metabolism.
source: Our observation that SSB-ssDNA is macroscopically organized and regulated through microscopic interactions is surprisingly similar to the most basic organization of eukaryotic chromatin and highlights the important role of SSB, not simply as a kinetic trap for ssDNA, but as an organizational and regulatory scaffold during DNA metabolism (Shereda et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data supported by citations.

claim: The organizational and regulatory role of SSB is likely controlled by the acidic, intrinsically disordered C-terminal tail of SSB, which is required for cooperative binding of SSB to ssDNA.
source: This organizational and regulatory role is likely controlled by the acidic, intrinsically disordered C-terminal tail of SSB, which is required for cooperative binding of SSB to ssDNA (Kozlov et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Recent studies have identified a cadre of proteins, including the χ subunit of DNA polymerase III, PriA, PriB, RecG, RNaseHI, Exonuclease I, and RecO, that bind to the C-terminal tail of SSB and either remodel the SSB-ssDNA complex or regulate enzymatic ssDNA metabolism.
source: Recent studies have identified a cadre of proteins, including the χ subunit of DNA polymerase III, PriA, PriB, RecG, RNaseHI, Exonuclease I, and RecO, that bind to the C-terminal tail of SSB and either remodel the SSB-ssDNA complex or regulate enzymatic ssDNA metabolism (Cadman and McGlynn, 2004; Shereda et al., 2007, 2008; Lu and Keck, 2008; Kozlov et al., 2010a, 2010b, 2015; Wessel et al., 2013; Bhattacharyya et al., 2014; Petzold et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: These many proteins may regulate access to ssDNA by binding to SSB and altering either compaction/de-compaction most likely by perturbing the microscopic binding state of SSB.
source: Extrapolating from our observations in this work, these many proteins may regulate access to ssDNA by binding to SSB and altering either compaction/de-compaction most likely by perturbing the microscopic binding state of SSB.
evidence: This is an extrapolation from the experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: The condensation of SSB-ssDNA occurs not only with increasing osmolality, but also by the addition of RecO, which binds directly to SSB, in the absence and presence of RecR.
source: Indeed, we demonstrate that this condensation occurs not only with increasing osmolality, but also by the addition of RecO, which binds directly to SSB, in the absence and presence of RecR (Ryzhikov et al., 2011).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Altering the macromolecular state of SSB-ssDNA by bridging distant sites could reduce the three-dimensional space required to facilitate homology-dependent annealing of ssDNA.
source: In the case of RecO and RecOR, altering this macromolecular state by bridging distant sites could reduce the three-dimensional space required to facilitate homology-dependent annealing of ssDNA (Berg et al., 1981; Forget and Kowalczykowski, 2012), which occurs by a second order kinetic process (Berg et al., 1981; Kantake et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2006; Bell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Homology-dependent annealing of ssDNA occurs by a second order kinetic process.
source: In the case of RecO and RecOR, altering this macromolecular state by bridging distant sites could reduce the three-dimensional space required to facilitate homology-dependent annealing of ssDNA (Berg et al., 1981; Forget and Kowalczykowski, 2012), which occurs by a second order kinetic process (Berg et al., 1981; Kantake et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2006; Bell et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: RecO has been shown to slow the rate of one-dimensional diffusion, or sliding, of SSB on ssDNA.
source: Similarly, RecO has been shown to slow the rate of one-dimensional diffusion, or sliding, of SSB on ssDNA (Zhou et al., 2011), which is consistent with the small energy contribution of RecO and RecOR binding we observe here, where RecO contributes an additional ∼1–2 kBT per SSB tetramer.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: By slowing the rate of diffusion of SSB on ssDNA, RecO might facilitate both annealing and RecA nucleation by increasing the lifetime of transiently exposed ssDNA.
source: By slowing the rate of diffusion of SSB on ssDNA, RecO might facilitate both annealing and RecA nucleation by increasing the lifetime of transiently exposed ssDNA.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data and previous knowledge.

claim: The long range interactions induced by RecR could be due to phasing of SSB via its interaction with RecO, creating microscopic gaps on the ssDNA that allow distant sites with micro-homology to anneal, forming intramolecular secondary structure.
source: The long range interactions induced by RecR could also be due to phasing of SSB via its interaction with RecO, creating microscopic gaps on the ssDNA that allow distant sites with micro-homology to anneal, forming intramolecular secondary structure (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data.

claim: In its biological context, the microscopic gaps created by RecOR could facilitate the nucleation of RecA filaments during homologous recombination by exposing short segments of ssDNA between SSB tetramers.
source: In its biological context, these microscopic gaps could also facilitate the nucleation of RecA filaments during homologous recombination by exposing short segments of ssDNA between SSB tetramers, either by inducing a conformational change that physically disrupts the SSB-ssDNA complex to create gaps or by increasing the lifetime of transiently exposed ssDNA created during SSB sliding along the ssDNA (Bell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data and cited work.

claim: SSBAF488 is particularly suitable for single molecule measurements due to its relative photostability.
